items.title: Run independent coding jobs without a companion or host-wide slot ceiling
items.description: ## Outcome and real setup Any companion can start four or more independent coding jobs on the established Mac. The Hub admits approved jobs without a per-companion or host-wide job-count limit. Providers and harnesses govern model-request throttling. ## Smallest useful implementation Remove slot-based admission from the worker, coordinator and UI. Version endpoint/state contracts and page active jobs independently of result-size and queue bounds. Replace slot-derived setup deadlines with per-job setup progress. Preserve compatibility with older workers that advertise a finite capacity. Align the Apartment room's #2034 handoff with job attribution. ## Behavior and protections to preserve The owner supersedes #2028's runtime slot policy. Keep a distinct worktree, cancellation target and attempt identity per job, serialize conflicting git setup, preserve per-run limits and the existing Mac test admission rules. Display resource errors truthfully. A UI page size is never a dispatch limit. ## Observable acceptance and planned evidence - [ ] One companion starts at least four independent jobs while another companion can submit one. No job waits for an invented Hub slot. Open more jobs than fit on one page and locate every job. - [ ] Under a slow provider, only the harness-reported status describes throttling. A real resource or spawn failure identifies the affected attempt while siblings and the Hub continue. Measure Mac load and Hub responsiveness during installed acceptance. - [ ] Exercise concurrent setup in one repository, disk/setup failure, cancellation, disconnect, late child exit and restart. Preserve existing worktrees and one active writer per attempt. An older worker still receives only work it can admit. ## Starting point Replace the slot assumptions in the worker, coordinator and their wire fixtures on the same contract comparison. This work depends on [#2109](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/2109). Delivery target: reviewed integrated source and disposable acceptance. [#2115](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/2115) owns the installed checks on a single compatible release for [#2105](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/2105). Include the focused second review for changes to credential handling, storage migration, writer exclusion or device-command safety when that boundary changes. items.title: FixFinder reads the photo and suggests a description
items.description: ## Problem / Motivation FixFinder doesn't read photos yet. Every report gets the same sample answer ("Pothole"), whatever the photo shows, so the team can't tell whether the core flow works on real problems. ## Desired Outcome After the user takes or chooses a photo, FixFinder reads it and suggests a short description of the problem, like "Overflowing trash can," which Result shows. When FixFinder can't tell what the problem is, or can't reach its photo reader, it says so plainly in its own words and offers clear next steps. ## Acceptance Criteria - [ ] A photo of a real problem leads to Result showing a description FixFinder made from that photo: a short phrase that says what the problem is the way a person would. - [ ] Result's placeholder note no longer covers the description. It still marks the responsible party and source as sample output. - [ ] When FixFinder can't tell what the problem is, Working shows "reading the photo" as not worked, with the notice "FixFinder couldn't tell what the problem is from this photo." and two next steps: Retake photo (main) and Describe it yourself. - [ ] Describe it yourself lets the user type a short description and carries on to Result with the same photo and location. - [ ] When FixFinder can't reach its photo reader (no connection, no answer in time), Working says so in its own words and offers Try again with the same photo, and Describe it yourself. - [ ] Words from the photo reader itself, such as an apology or an explanation, never appear on screen as the description. ## Constraints / Non-goals - Lands with or after #12, so the first real call is already recorded with its cost. - The team can still build and test against the stand-in, with no real AI calls, as README's AI usage section asks. - Out of scope: saying why FixFinder couldn't read the photo (too dark, too blurry). - Out of scope: finding the responsible party for real. That's its own issue. - Out of scope: editing the suggested description on Result. That's #16. ## Context - Step one of the two-step AI flow the team settled on: describe the photo, then find the responsible party from the description, the photo, and the location. - Wrong or bad descriptions seen while building go in docs/ai-failure-log.md. - Serves invariant 2 (AI is part of how FixFinder works) and invariant 7 (the user knows whether FixFinder's steps worked). The failure path follows Nielsen 9 (help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors).

items.description: ## What Audit Alexi static model catalog for missing Claude Opus 4.5/4.6/4.7 dated variants and verify bash tree-sitter tag extraction completeness. ## Why Aider PR #5173 (2026-10-26) expanded the Anthropic model list with recent Claude variants: `claude-opus-4-5-20251101`, `claude-opus-4-6-20260205`, `claude-opus-4-7-20260416`, `claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219`. Alexi's static fallback catalog (`ORCHESTRATION_MODELS` in `src/providers/sapOrchestration.ts`) may be missing these if SAP AI Core exposes them. Additionally, Aider added bash tree-sitter tags for repomap (function definitions, variable declarations); verify Alexi's bash tree-sitter support is complete. ## How - Audit `src/providers/sapOrchestration.ts`: - Check `ORCHESTRATION_MODELS` array for missing entries: `claude-opus-4-5-20251101`, `claude-opus-4-6-20260205`, `claude-opus-4-7-20260416`, `claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219` - If SAP AI Core deployment catalog includes these variants, add to `ORCHESTRATION_MODELS` array - Add corresponding entries to `ORCHESTRATION_MODEL_METADATA` map with capabilities: `{ supportsVision: true, supportsThinking: true, maxOutputTokens: 16384, contextWindow: 200000 }` (adjust context window per variant) - Audit `src/tool/tools/definitions.ts`: - Check bash tree-sitter support: verify function tag extraction (`function foo() { ... }`) and variable tag extraction (`VAR=value`) - If extraction incomplete, add missing tag queries (port from Aider's bash tree-sitter PR #5132 if needed) - Create `tests/providers/modelCatalog-variants.test.ts`: - Unit test: verify new model ids resolve to correct capabilities (vision: true, thinking: true, maxTokens, contextWindow) - Integration test: verify routing can select new variants when available - Update `docs/PROVIDERS.md`: - Document newly added variants with capabilities and use cases - Note that dated variants (e.g. `claude-opus-4-7-20260416`) are pinned snapshots for reproducibility ## Done when - [ ] Audit complete: documented whether SAP AI Core exposes Claude Opus 4.5/4.6/4.7 dated variants - [ ] If variants exist: `ORCHESTRATION_MODELS` updated with new entries - [ ] If variants exist: `ORCHESTRATION_MODEL_METADATA` updated with capabilities (vision, thinking, maxTokens, contextWindow) - [ ] Bash tree-sitter audit complete: verified function/variable tag extraction works (or added missing queries if gap found) - [ ] `tests/providers/modelCatalog-variants.test.ts` exists and passes (new model ids resolve to correct capabilities)

items.title: t19358: Add prompt-cache keep-alive to the OpenCode v2 provider-auth adapter
items.description: ## Task Give OpenCode v2 the prompt-cache keep-alive that PR #40256 added for v1, so long tool calls stop forcing full cache rebuilds there too. Full task brief and audit context ## Task Brief ## What Give OpenCode v2 the prompt-cache keep-alive that PR #40256 added for v1, so long tool calls stop forcing full cache rebuilds there too. ## Why On v1, PR #40256 records each completed agent request. While a tool runs longer than the 5-minute cache TTL, it re-sends that request with `max_tokens: 1`. In one worker fleet, about 29.9% of cache writes followed 5–60 minute gaps; this removes them. The v2 adapter does not record requests, so v2 sessions still pay those rebuilds. OpenCode v1 is the active host today, so this is not urgent. Without it, the saving disappears when hosts move to v2. ## Dependency Blocked by #40251: PR #40256 adds `cache-keepalive.mjs` and the v1 wiring. Start only after that PR has merged to `main`. A worker that finds `cache-keepalive.mjs` missing should stop as blocked rather than recreate it. ## How - Files to modify: - `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/v2-provider-auth.mjs`: in `createHttpResponseHook`, after a 2xx Anthropic response, call `cacheKeepalive.recordRequest(event.sessionID, , , status)`. - `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/v2.mjs`: wire tool start/finish to `cacheKeepalive.toolStarted` / `toolFinished`, matching `index.mjs` (`rg -n "cacheKeepalive" .agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/index.mjs`). - `cache-keepalive.mjs` and `provider-auth.mjs` are in scope only to export or share an existing helper with v2, such as a host-neutral send builder. Do not change v1 behaviour. - Reference pattern: - `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/provider-auth.mjs`: see `sendCacheKeepalive` and the `cacheKeepalive.recordRequest(` call. Refreshes re-run the same body transforms and auth headers as the real request. - `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/cache-keepalive.mjs`: `createCacheKeepalive({ send })` is host-neutral. Reuse it rather than duplicating the scheduler. - Constraint: v2 uses request/response hooks, not a fetch wrapper. The `send` callback must issue its own `fetch` with a freshly resolved access token. Reuse `anthropicRequest()` / `transformedBody()` so the refresh body matches the cached prefix byte for byte. Fail open on any error. - Hazard: the rotation probe loads plugin modules in an isolated VM with an allowlist (`.agents/scripts/oauth-pool-rotation-probe.mjs`). If v2 imports a new module, keep `tests/test-oauth-pool-ro

items.title: Architectuurscan periodiek en onbemand, met één beslisissue
items.description: ### Beschrijving Een architectuurscan (een skill die kandidaten voor verbetering zoekt: hotspots, ondiepe modules, dubbele bronnen van waarheid) loont, maar draait alleen als iemand eraan denkt. In paia leverde de eerste scan vijf issues en drie aanvullingen op. Lighthouse heeft zo'n skill nog niet; de bron is paia's `/paia-improve-codebase-architecture` (paia #746). Dit issue brengt de skill naar `pack/core` en laat de scan periodiek en onbemand draaien, in elke repo die het aanzet: - **headless modus**: de kandidaten komen in de body van precies één beslisissue, niet in een chatantwoord; - **eerst ontdubbelen**: een kandidaat die al onder een open issue valt, staat onder "nog open uit eerdere scans" met het nummer; - **claims nagetrokken**: elke claim is gemarkeerd als *nagemeten* (met commando en uitkomst), *niet nagemeten* of *niet meetbaar vanaf hier*; - **een mislukte run** maakt geen half issue. Wacht op #121: de scan is een geplande run. Herkomst: [paia #1205](https://github.com/CorneeldH/personal_ai_agent/issues/1205). Ontwerp: [spec](https://github.com/CorneeldH/lighthouse/blob/main/docs/developer/planning/specs/2026-11-16-zelflerende-lighthouse-design.md). ### Acceptatiecriteria - [ ] De architectuurscan-skill staat in `pack/core` (Claude- en agents-variant), overgenomen uit paia en ontdaan van paia-paden; interactief gebruik blijft werken. - [ ] De scan draait als geplande run (#121) op een configureerbaar schema, standaard eens per kwartaal. - [ ] Een geslaagde run schrijft precies één issue met het label voor een besluit; de kandidaten worden pas issues als de gebruiker ze kiest. - [ ] Kandidaten die onder een open issue vallen, staan met nummer onder "nog open uit eerdere scans". - [ ] Elke claim draagt een van de drie markeringen. - [ ] Een mislukte run (geen auth, time-out, lege uitvoer) maakt geen issue en eindigt niet-nul. - [ ] Tokenverbruik per run staat in de telemetrie. ### Definition of Done - [ ] Code reviewed - [ ] Tests geschreven en groen - [ ] Documentatie bijgewerkt - [ ] Geen bekende bugs

items.title: Advanced/Services: configurable PDS, AppView and service endpoints instead of hardcoded Bluesky hosts
items.description: Part of the Advanced submenu (#93). All network calls currently go through @atproto/api with the default Bluesky service. Make every host configurable through one typed services module, surfaced in **Advanced → Services**. ## What to build - A single services config per account: PDS URL, AppView URL, optional relay/Jetstream URL, feed generator endpoints, labeler endpoints. Persisted with the session store (AsyncStorage today) and exportable. - **Advanced → Services** screen: current values, a "Use defaults" button, and a per-slot "Test connection" action. - Point the Agent/AppAgent at the configured service instead of the implicit default. Anything using appView proxy endpoints should read the configured AppView. - Existing sessions keep working unchanged after the update (config defaults must match current behaviour). ## Alternatives research - The [self-hosting guide](https://atproto.com/guides/self-hosting) covers what exists at each tier: PDSs are practical to self-host; AppViews and relays are heavier, which is why independent operators matter for client choice. - [threddyrex/atproto-links](https://github.com/threddyrex/atproto-links) collects implementations of PDSs, relays and AppViews. - Known independent implementations to test against: the reference Bluesky PDS, [millipds](https://openpds.tijs.org/), Cirrus, Cocoon, Arroba, Custos (all listed on the [OpenPDS directory](https://openpds.tijs.org/)), [rsky](https://hysenlabs.com/projects/blacksky-algorithms-rsky) (Rust PDS/relay/feedgen/labeler) and [AppViewLite](https://github.com/alnkesq/AppViewLite). ## Acceptance - No Bluesky host is hardcoded outside the default config values. - Changing any endpoint from Advanced → Services takes effect without an app restart, and is reversible.

items.title: Reduce W4 DSP work and W5 audio deadline misses
items.description: - W5 offline at 0.967–0.979× with exact original PCM. At 128 frames, the limiting interval needs 1.57–1.60× DSP speed. W1 and W5 still underrun on OCTA-CAPTURE at 44.1 kHz with a 128-frame ring and a 16-frame period. - The same native DSP image spends 43–47% of sampled cycles in grouped regions and 15–16% on precise parallel instructions across the W1 live failure and the busiest W4/W5 offline windows. Reduce both. See PR #45 and ACCEPTANCE.tsv. - Verify original PCM and device clocks, then qualify regular live buffers with zero underruns and lost MIDI.

items.title: Support `;;` line comments for Lisp tooling and coding agents
items.description: ## Problem Elle source files use the `.lisp` extension, but Elle line comments begin with `#`. Generic Lisp syntax highlighters therefore render `#` / `##` comment blocks as code instead of comments. This is especially visible in agent-facing Elle code. For example, I'm writting an agent usign elle-lisp, my `cordis-pi/bundled/` currently contains 26 `.lisp` files with roughly 1,188 `#` / `##` comment lines, and those files are frequently displayed in coding-agent transcripts. There is a related generation problem: coding agents have a strong Lisp-family prior and commonly write `;` or `;;` comments. In Elle, however, a single `;` is the splice operator. A plausible-looking Lisp comment can therefore become executable syntax rather than merely receiving the wrong highlighting. A custom Elle editor grammar would improve supported editors, but it would not fix generic `.lisp` renderers, Markdown code blocks, or agent-generated source. ## Proposal Accept `;;` as an additional line-comment prefix: Keep the existing syntax unchanged: In other words: - `;; ...` → comment to end of line - `# ...` → existing comment syntax, retained for compatibility - `;expr` → existing splice syntax - `,;expr` → existing unquote-splicing syntax Agent-facing examples and integrations could then prefer `;;`, without requiring a whole-tree migration or deprecating `#`. ## Why `;;` rather than changing single `;` Replacing single `;` would conflict with Elle's splice operator and require a breaking language change. A whitespace-sensitive distinction such as `;expr` versus `; comment` would also leave `;comment` ambiguous. `;;` is unambiguous, conventional for full-line Lisp comments, and already recognized by generic Lisp highlighters. Adjacent splice operators are not a useful executable form today, so this should be a small compatibility addition rather than a splice redesign. ## Implementation surface The likely affected areas are small: - lexer: emit `Token::Comment` when a token-boundary `;;` is encountered; - formatter/comment preservation; - syntax documentation and coming-from guides; - tests proving that `;;` comments work while `;expr` and `,;expr` retain their current meanings; - downstream structural editors/lexers such as `elle-edit` (A tool I'd like to share in the future which is specially designed to be used by agent to edit elle-lisp). This would align Elle's `.lisp` files with existing tooling and reduce a recurring source of coding-agent mistakes without removing a

items.title: [Contracts] Add a migration status view with the executable ledger
items.description: ## Summary `get_migration_snapshot` returns the target adapter, snapshot value, and snapshot ledger, but not the earliest ledger at which `migrate_adapter` can execute. A client must recompute the cooldown from a constant. ## Motivation Operators and dashboards need one read that answers whether a pending migration is ready. Recomputing the threshold off chain can drift if the contract constant changes or a client uses the wrong value. ## Proposed Solution Add a read-only migration status view that returns the snapshot plus the earliest executable ledger and the remaining ledgers. Return a clear empty state when no migration is pending. Keep the existing snapshot getter for compatibility. Cover pending, ready, and empty states with tests. ## Scope | Field | Value | | ----------------- | ------- | | Area | Contracts | | Protocol affected | Both | | Network | testnet and mainnet | | Breaking change? | No | ## Alternatives Considered Adding fields to the snapshot type would change a stored value and require a migration path. A separate view is additive and does not alter storage. ## Acceptance Criteria - [ ] One read returns the snapshot, earliest ledger, and remaining ledgers - [ ] The view reports an empty state when no migration is pending - [ ] The existing snapshot getter is unchanged - [ ] Tests cover pending, ready, and empty states - [ ] `cargo test --workspace` and `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` pass ## Additional Context The snapshot type and cooldown are in `packages/contracts/vault/src/storage.rs` and `packages/contracts/vault/src/lib.rs`. The cooldown must not be shortened. The migration keeper in `packages/stellar-sdk-helpers/src/migration-keeper.ts` is a likely consumer.

items.title: Ask HN: Am I the only one whose AI hype is cooling down a lot?
items.description: I am in the industry for 15+ years, studied CS, and actually, never really "liked" programming. It was a means to an end. I have written about programming (and published books), so don't get me wrong: I like the craft and I miss the sense of accomplishment after hours and days of struggling and fixing a problem with 2 lines of code. What I see in my personal spending and habits: I get free tokens from my company, and I spent between 3k-5k a month at the start of the year. Models got cheaper, but also: The usefullness ran its course a little bit for me. I still don't write code by hand, but when doing research, finding solutions, even some decisions (using Opus 5.5 and Astra 6.2 for example) are more and more questionable. I handed large research tasks to models, but even small questions like: "What do you think about these PR comments pointing out issues" (I need to be vague, working for a larger company), it didn't find even basic facts I found via Google and reading the docs for 2mins. I usually did higher level thinking, researched with the model, and then went to the implementation phase. But lately, I am not happy with both the research results (I continuesly have to narrow it down, go back, refine... I spend a day or 2 days refining, which in the end, I can do by myself now and actually feel a sense of accomplishment). Even the implementation isn't all that great. Maybe my bar for acceptable work is higher now, since these tools are not "magic" anymore. I think I gave them more leeway in the beginning because they wowed me. But now... not so much anymore. I even dread opening up Claude Code or Codex and I'd rather read and write code myself, and just give them smaller tasks, or once I nailed it down, I let a large chunk of code write by a model (because it "types" faster...). Am I alone? I read a lot of think pieces, I have agents working on my private dedicated server to maintain my machine and set up my self-hosting services. But more and more, I'd rather.... do it myself again, be more precise, and use it as a workhorse instead of a thinking researcher.

items.title: Ask HN: Everything will get breached. How do you limit the blast radius?
items.description: Got another breach email this morning, this travel operator had my passport number and travel history stored. At this point I feel every service we use is going to get dumped eventually. I consider unique passwords and hardware 2FA as no brainers, they stop credential stuffing, but they don't help when a service leaks your actual identity. There are just so many services that require personal data like your passport number, phone number etc. And I think the fallout will only get worse as agentic workflows and local models become more mainstream and people start giving them more and more personal data. Assuming every vendor database is basically public eventually, how are you actually limiting the blast radius without turning everyday life into a massive faff?

items.title: Ask HN: How are tech recruiters assessed on their recruiting skills?
items.description: I've been working in tech for around 10 years but I have absolutely no experience at all in tech recruiting. However I have had the experience (well, often displeasure) of going through tech recruiters and the tech hiring process when applying for jobs during my career. As with probably many of you, I'm quite frustrated with how tech hiring has been in the last year or two during the AI/LLM era. It's incredibly frustrating to send tens to hundreds of CVs for applications you would be an excellent fit for and seeing the roles go to less qualified candidates, or candidates who just end up leaving after a few months or a year. This has left me wondering how tech recruiters are assessed on their recruiting skills and retaining qualified talent within their respective organizations. For those of you who work or have worked in tech recruiting, or have insider knowledge regarding how tech recruiters are assessed, could you share some insight into how tech recruiters are assessed? Is there any kind of follow-up regarding the performance of the people have hired, retention rates, and so on?

items.title: Ask HN: Where the company's employees launch the tools that Claude created
items.description: Hi everyone, Here is a situation: In a typical company these days, many employees are creating tools using AI (Claude & Cursor) to help with their work. They run these tools on their own computers, which no one else can use or on a builder platform with a public URL and either no login or a hand-rolled one the agent wrote. Question: Where do they run this? Who can see it? What happens if an employee leaves the company?

items.title: Ask HN: Should Uber Ratings Decay over Time?
items.description: I’ve been thinking about how platforms like Uber calculate reputation scores, and I believe there’s a fundamental flaw in how historical ratings are treated. Uber calculates passenger ratings using the last 500 rated trips, regardless of when those trips occurred. In my case, I have 455 ratings, 426 of which are five stars (93.6%). My overall rating is 4.86. What bothers me isn’t the score itself, but the underlying methodology. A negative rating from five years ago can carry exactly the same weight as one received yesterday. And if you’re an infrequent user who hasn’t accumulated 500 ratings, that negative feedback could influence your reputation for years. This raises an interesting question: Should reputation systems measure your historical average, or should they attempt to represent who you are today? One possible solution is exponential time decay: Weight = 2^(-t/H) Where t is the age of the rating and H is a half-life, perhaps 12 months. Under that approach, a rating from one year ago would carry 50% of its original weight, and one from two years ago just 25%. Of course, this introduces other challenges. How do you prevent someone with a history of poor behaviour from simply waiting for their reputation to recover? How do you maintain statistical confidence for infrequent users? Would Bayesian smoothing or a minimum effective sample size help? There’s also a broader philosophical question around the right to be forgotten. Should digital reputation systems indefinitely preserve the consequences of historical assessments, particularly when those assessments are subjective and potentially no longer representative? I’m curious how others would approach this. * Is a rolling window of 500 ratings statistically defensible without considering time? * Would exponential decay produce a fairer and more predictive reputation score? * Should platforms expose both a lifetime rating and a recent-behaviour rating? * Are there better approaches already being used in other reputation systems? I’d be particularly interested in perspectives from people who’ve worked on marketplace ranking, trust and safety, or reputation algorithms. It seems like a relatively simple mathematical change, but one with potentially significant implications for fairness across digital platforms.

items.title: Ask HN: Are startups today worth it even in a best case scenario?
items.description: I'm gonna open this with the disclaimer that this is purely a financial and risk comparison post. No one is complaining that we are poorly compensated. It is good to discuss compensation so we can make informed and educated decisions when deciding how to commit the next few years of our lives. A close friend of mine joined an AI startup (being intentionally vague) around 1.5 years ago and despite the company doing extremely well on valuation, I'm surprised at how he's not really better off than just working at a large tech company. Concrete numbers for the startup: -200k salary -Equity grant over 4 years is 500k -The company's valuation has since went from single billions to tens of billions, leaving him with a 10x multiplier when looking only at valuation. After you account for dilution, it's closer to 6x. -Liquidity event annually allows you to sell 10% of your vested shares Big tech at a similar years of experience is around 400-500k total comp, and the RSU component is generally liquid. For example sake and ease of calculation, if you assume that my friend's entire equity was vested, and he was able to sell 10% of it, it would amount to approximately $300k/liquidity event, which brings him to around 500k a year as well (200k + 300k). In reality, he's really only able to access $300k/4 since that's all he has vested and that brings him closer to $75k for this liquidity event. There are a lot of variables I'm leaving out obviously such as potential future value, IPO, etc., but the thing that is surprising to me overall is that this is a close to best case outcome, yet the employee doesn't really end up any better off than big tech due to lack of liquidity and dilution. I mean I get it, impact, interesting work, etc. -- the qualitative measures -- aren't really accounted for, but I'm not looking to make a wholistic comparison. This brings me to the question: Is the risk in a startup ever justified for a lower level employee (engineer, Product Manager, Program Manager, etc.)?
